reason: The row unit is a utility x forecast-year window, and the entity that recurs is the EIA utility number. One utility contributes up to three holdout rows (forecast years 2022-2024), and their labels are dependent by construction: each label compares CY Y+1 SAIDI excluding major event days with the median of CY Y-3..Y-1 (reproduction/build.py:1084, 1117, 1124, 1132), so adjacent cohorts of one utility share two of three baseline years and the outcome value of cohort Y is the lag-1 feature of cohort Y+2 (build.py:1114, 1140). utility_cohort_id is unique per row (build.py:1133, 1186-1192) and is not an independence unit. Training metadata agree: in public train.csv the label's one-way ICC is 0.219 within utility_id (758 utilities, mean 3.2 rows) versus 0.026 within state, 0.023 within state x forecast_year and 0.001 within forecast_year, and P(positive in cohort Y+1 | positive in cohort Y) is 0.399 against 0.158 unconditional. utility_id is a declared non-predictor carry column written to every split (build.py:15, 30, 963-966). Chosen from source meaning, pinned code and public training rows only, before any holdout scoring and without holdout rows or metrics.
limitations: Cross-utility dependence from shared weather and regional conditions in the same year is not captured. Training-label ICC within state x forecast_year is small (0.023; within single cohorts the state ICC ranges from -0.027 to 0.056) but with roughly a dozen rows per state-year it is not zero in aggregate, so utility-clustered intervals may be somewhat too narrow. A state-clustered interval is a coarser sensitivity check, not a replacement: 5 of 814 utilities in public train/eval carry more than one state across cohorts, so state does not strictly nest utility_id.

The holdout has only three decision dates (forecast years 2022, 2023, 2024). Year-level common shocks are a three-cluster effect that utility-level resampling cannot represent; forecast_year is not usable as a cluster key.

utility_id is the EIA utility number of the filing entity. Operating companies under one corporate parent, and utilities sharing a generation-and-transmission cooperative or a common outage-management practice, are separate ids; no parent or affiliation column exists in the data, so that dependence is unmodelled.

The build drops a utility-year when the utility files more than one row, and drops cohorts spanning a change of utility number or reporting standard (build.py:799-805, 1000-1003, 1094-1101). An entity that was renumbered after a merger would appear as two ids; this was not checked.

Dependence figures come from public train rows (forecast years 2016-2019) only. Holdout rows were not read, so the number of holdout utilities and the rows-per-utility distribution there are unverified; presence of utility_id in the holdout file is inferred from build.py, not observed.
